idea.why: Two independent gather-and-interpret branches and one editor agent that only composes, with presentation left to a separate render step. Each agent owns one concern and is told to copy stats rather than recompute them. The conceptual gap is that a dashboard is realised as an emailed page rather than something viewable on demand.

structure.why: Aggregate collapses many items so each agent runs once, structured output parsers instead of prompt-begging for JSON, and the purpose-built HTML node rather than a Code node. The merge is close to decorative since the composer pulls data through node references. The HTML node carries a lot of inline map, join and regex logic in one expression blob.

connections.why: Close to textbook: the trigger fans out to the two genuinely independent fetches instead of chaining them, each branch is chained only where a real dependency exists, and the two streams rejoin at a single merge before the composer. One shared model feeds all three agents while each gets its own parser because the schemas genuinely differ.

answer.why: Daily run, both sources, sorted into urgent, needs-reply and FYI plus a timed day plan, then a real dashboard with stat tiles, priorities, agenda and watchouts. Empty-state fallbacks and angle-bracket stripping mean it degrades sensibly. Weakened by a dark-theme page whose CSS lives entirely in a head style block.

appraisal: This finds the right shape almost immediately: two independent branches fanned out from one trigger, a merge where they genuinely rejoin, and a composer that only writes copy while a purpose-built HTML node owns presentation. The supporting choices show real fluency: Aggregate so the agents run once rather than per message, structured output parsers instead of hoping for clean JSON, one shared model across three agents, and a sticky note naming exactly which slots a user must fill. The soft spots are the Merge, which acts only as a synchronisation barrier since the composer reads through node references anyway, and a dashboard whose entire stylesheet sits in a head block that many mail clients strip. A knowledgeable user would fix the delivery first, then either read from the merged item or drop the Merge.
